title: Prejudice and Discrimination
keyIdea: Prejudice is judging or disliking someone before you know them, because of a group they belong to, such as their race, religion, disability or sex. It is a feeling or attitude. Discrimination is an action: treating someone worse because of who they are. A stereotype (an idea about a whole group) can feed prejudice, and prejudice can lead to discrimination. Being treated differently is not always discrimination; the test is whether it is because of who they are. Discrimination hurts the person, the people around them and the whole community. In Great Britain the Equality Act 2010 protects nine characteristics by law. You can stand against it safely: include the person, calmly say it is not fair, and tell a trusted adult.

kid: The word prejudice means to pre-judge: to decide what someone is like before you know them. It is a feeling, like not liking the new boy because of where his family comes from.

Discrimination is what someone does. It is treating a person worse because of who they are. A club that will not let a deaf girl join is discriminating. So is a guard who follows a boy round a shop just because he is Black.

Not every difference is unfair. If Sam misses the try-out, it is fair not to pick him. If Priya gets extra time because she has dyslexia, that helps her have a fair chance. Ask: is it because of who they are?

Discrimination does real harm. The person can feel hurt, alone and scared to come to school. Their friends and family hurt too, and the whole class trusts each other less. You can help: include them, say calmly that it is not fair, and tell an adult.
adult: This topic sits in PSHE and the statutory Relationships Education guidance, which asks pupils to understand respect for others who are different and how stereotypes can be unfair. Pupils of 9 to 11 should define prejudice and discrimination in their own words. They should describe the harm it does and name an action they can take.

The terms build in a chain. A stereotype is a fixed idea about a group. Prejudice is a negative attitude or feeling toward a person because of their group. Discrimination is unfair treatment because of who someone is. It is an action, so it can happen without anyone saying a word. The Equality Act 2010 names nine protected characteristics: age, disability, gender reassignment, marriage and civil partnership, pregnancy and maternity, race, religion or belief, sex, and sexual orientation.

Common mistakes: calling a private feeling discrimination, when it is prejudice until someone acts on it; thinking any different treatment is discrimination, when the question is why; treating support such as extra time as unfair; and calling hurtful remarks just a joke. A common error with older children is to think that standing up means being a hero. Be careful to stress safe actions: include, speak up calmly, report.

In the lab, learners drag cards to build the chain from idea to feeling to action. They sort cases by whether the reason is who the person is. They open the ripples of harm round one girl and shield the nine protected characteristics. Last, they choose the safe, helpful responses to two scenes, one of them online.

familyTip: When a news story, film or playground tale involves someone being treated unfairly, ask: was it because of who they are, or something they did? Then ask: what could someone nearby have done to help, safely?

visual.caption: Prejudice or discrimination? Drag each card, or tap it and then tap a box.

items: Dislikes the new girl because she is from Romania
Won’t pass the ball to the boy in a turban
Feels nervous of old people without knowing any
Tells a girl she can’t join because she is deaf
Thinks badly of a family because of their religion
Pays a woman less than a man for the same job
Distrusts someone because of their skin colour
Refuses to let a wheelchair user into the club

lab.caption: Flagship lab: build idea → feeling → action, test the reason, open the ripples of harm, shield the 9 protected characteristics and choose safe ways to help.

practice.prompt: Ella does not like Muslim children, but she has never said or done anything about it. What is this?
practice.hint: Has anyone been treated worse yet, or is it still a feeling?
practice.explain: It is prejudice: a feeling against people because of their religion. It becomes discrimination if she treats someone worse.

practice.prompt: A poster shows {n} of the protected characteristics in the Equality Act 2010. How many are missing from the poster?
practice.hint: The Act lists 9 protected characteristics in total.
practice.explain: There are 9 in the Act, so 9 − {n} = {=9-n} are missing.

practice.prompt: Jas is not picked for the football team because he did not come to the try-out. Is this discrimination?
choices: No, it is about what he did
Yes, being left out is always discrimination
practice.hint: Ask: is it because of who he is?
practice.explain: Missing the try-out is about what he did, not who he is. That is a fair reason, so it is not discrimination.

practice.prompt: After hearing {n} jokes about one group, Tom starts to dislike children from that group without knowing any of them. What is this feeling?
practice.hint: Is it something he feels, or something he does to someone?
practice.explain: It is prejudice. The {n} jokes fed a stereotype, and the stereotype fed a feeling against people he has never met.

pool.prompt: A club will not let a girl join because she is deaf. What is this?
choices: Fair, because it is their club
pool.hint: Did someone act, and was it because of who she is?
pool.explain: The club acted and treated her worse because of her disability. That is discrimination, and the Equality Act protects disability.

pool.prompt: Priya gets extra time in tests because she has dyslexia. Is that unfair to the others?
choices: No, it gives her a fair chance
Yes, everyone must be treated the same
pool.hint: What is the extra time for?
pool.explain: The extra time helps her show what she knows. Support for a need is fair; it is not discrimination against anyone.

pool.prompt: Kofi is followed round a shop {n} times this month, though he has never taken anything. Why is this discrimination?
choices: He is treated worse because of his race
He goes to the shop a lot
pool.hint: Has he done anything to be followed for?
pool.explain: He has done nothing wrong in {n} visits. He is watched because he is Black, so he is treated worse for who he is.

pool.prompt: Some children mock a boy’s religion. The next day he does not want to come to school. What does this show?
pool.hint: Look at what happened to him afterwards.
pool.explain: He is so hurt that he wants to stay away. Remarks about who someone is cause real harm, even when called a joke.

pool.prompt: Your friend is left out because of her skin colour. What is a safe, helpful first step?
choices: Include her and tell a trusted adult
pool.hint: Choose something that helps her and keeps you safe.
pool.explain: Including her shows she is not alone, and an adult can stop it. Shouting can start a fight, and staying out leaves her alone.

pool.prompt: {n} children see a boy being mocked for his race. {k} of them step in safely to help. How many are still only watching?
pool.hint: Take the helpers away from everyone who saw it.
pool.explain: {n} − {k} = {=n-k} are still only watching. Each of them could also help safely, for example by telling an adult.

pool.prompt: Which one is a protected characteristic in the Equality Act 2010?
pool.hint: The Act lists 9, including age, race and disability.
pool.explain: Religion or belief is one of the 9. Being unkind about a team or hair colour is still wrong, but those are not on the list.

pool.prompt: Which shows the chain in the right order?
pool.hint: Start with an idea, then a feeling, then an action.
pool.explain: A stereotype is an idea, prejudice is the feeling it can feed, and discrimination is the unfair action that can follow.
